reasons.GPT-6.1 Sol::R04. Example stays at the d: The example stays in the exact task mechanics Dan called "two in the weeds": it walks through asking the AI to critique an opening and then judging that critique ("You save an opening and the request you gave the AI... compare how many of your checks its feedback passes"), sharpening rather than removing the critique-of-a-critique workflow and adding input-saving steps.
reasons.GPT-6 Sol::R04. Example stays at the def: The example is the workflow the rubric rules out: "Say you ask AI for feedback on an article opening. Give the same opening to several models, then check their feedback," which walks through checking a critique of an opening.
reasons.Sonnet 5.5::R01. Revised first sentence: The candidate paragraph's first sentence defines generic benchmarks with an unpacked metaphor — "Public benchmarks are like SAT scores: they tell you roughly how capable a model is..." — and only reaches the personal benchmark in the second and third sentences.
reasons.Opus 5.5::R04. Example stays at the defi: The example walks through the editing workflow the rubric warns against: "hand a model an opening you've already edited, ask for feedback, and check its answer the way you would."
reasons.GPT-5.6::R04. Example stays at the defin: The example walks through the critique workflow ("giving feedback on an article opening" goes to several models, then each critique is graded on "Did it catch that the headline buried the strongest claim?"), which is the task mechanics the rubric's FAIL condition names.

reasons.GPT-6 Sol::ai-wording: shared AI-tell phrases: its important to note
reasons.GPT-6 Sol::T01. Can the reader understan: The lead headline, "Banning provider counts made @Every drop useful timing figures elsewhere," uses the compressed shorthand "provider counts"; the reader must translate it (an outside copy editor's internal stage counts) to see what was targeted.
reasons.GPT-6 Sol::T05. Can the reader understan: The lead card's "a disclaimer scored worst, 0/3" is an unexplained metric, and the quote "names the class as loudly as a ban" relies on the undefined term "class," so the result is not fully clear without opening the sources.
reasons.Sonnet 5.5::ai-wording: shared AI-tell phrases: its important to note
reasons.Sonnet 5.5::T04. Does the body develop t: The face never says the suppression rule enumerated counts, so the jump from a jargon ban to "drop it everywhere" and then to an unintroduced "numbers rule" scoring "0 of 3" leaves the reader to reconstruct how the fix, the priming effect, and the score relate.
reasons.Sonnet 5.5::T05. Can the reader understa: The concrete result is never stated on the face — that planted timings dissolved into qualitative phrases in replies where nothing had failed — and it stands in an unexplained metric ("scored worst, 0 of 3", of what test or scale) plus the abstract quote "primes the model to drop it everywhere", so the reader must open the PR to learn what actually changed.
reasons.GPT-5.6::ai-wording: shared AI-tell phrases: its important to note
reasons.GPT-5.6::T02. Does the headline give the: The headline says only "other numbers" and does not say what useful information was lost; the face later says it was timing details, so the reader must supply the payoff.
reasons.GPT-5.6::T05. Can the reader understand: "main scored 3/3; variants scored 1/3, 0/3, and 1/3" and "Even 'never overrides the numbers rule' did worst" do not explain what the scores measure, what "main" is, or what the numbers rule is, so the reader must open the PR to understand the comparison.

reasons.GPT-6 Sol::S02b. Interesting headline: r: Its only proposed headline, 'Our CEO Wants Us to Use More Tokens,' is the exact example the rubric names as failing because it only reports an internal directive.
reasons.GPT-6 Sol::S03. Promise cashed out: Its headline frames the piece as a workplace story about a CEO directive, and it wrongly says the ROI dek promises a calculation instead of accepting qualitative returns.
reasons.GPT-6 Sol::S04a. Headline and dek connec: It criticizes the headline and dek separately and never addresses whether the dek develops the headline.
reasons.GPT-6 Sol::S06. Diagnoses delayed hook: Calling the first sentence 'slow' is vague; the feedback never notes that its point ('reining yourself in') arrives only at the end.
reasons.GPT-5.6::S02b. Interesting headline: rep: The recommended headline 'Spend First. Do the Token Math Later.' is essentially the rubric's failing example 'Spend the Tokens, Then Do the Math': it only says evaluation comes later and tells the reader nothing specific.
reasons.GPT-5.6::S04a. Headline and dek connect:: It critiques 'Token Math' and 'What's the ROI on experimentation?' separately and never says the dek fails to develop the headline or that their connection is unclear.
reasons.GPT-5.6::S05. Weasel words: The suggested opening states the statistic, then delays the ambition implication behind a familiar reaction: 'His reaction isn't to rein himself in. It's to wonder whether the rest of the team is experimenting ambitiously enough.'
reasons.GPT-5.6::S06. Diagnoses delayed hook: The offered opening still hooks on the cutback contrast, 'His reaction isn't to rein himself in,' which implies an unsupported default expectation to cut back for the CEO.

reasons.Opus 5.5::D01. First sentence answers th: Both versions open with "A personal benchmark is a test built from your own work", which describes what the benchmark is made of but not what it does for the reader, and it never mentions AI or choosing a model.
reasons.Opus 5.5::D02. Explain the terms the rea: Checks are explained with yes-or-no examples, but both versions end with "that correction becomes a new case and a new check" without ever explaining what a "case" is.
reasons.Opus 5.5::D03. Each sentence follows the: In the long version, "A personal benchmark is a reference check." leads straight into "And you don't have to build it by hand.", leaving the analogy unexplained and changing subject abruptly.
reasons.Opus 5.5::D04. Analogy clicks without al: Both versions say "A personal benchmark is a reference check" without showing how a reference check matches a personal benchmark, so the reader has to work out the comparison alone.
reasons.Opus 5.5::D06. Claims fit the supplied c: The short version says "it builds itself: every time you correct an AI, that correction becomes a new case and a new check," which presents a planned automatic capture as a current feature; the notes admit it is only the next step.
reasons.Opus 5.5::D07. Tests performance on your: Both versions present "A personal benchmark is a reference check" as the explanation, which is the secondhand-report framing rather than a work trial.
reasons.GPT-5.6::D01. First sentence answers the: The ANSWER.md paragraph opens with "A personal benchmark is a reference check for AI." This analogy has to be decoded and does not say what the reader gets from a personal benchmark.
reasons.GPT-5.6::D02. Explain the terms the read: The paragraph says models are scored "against checks drawn from your own judgment and corrections" but never explains what a "check" is.
reasons.GPT-5.6::D03. Each sentence follows the: The opening "reference check" framing is dropped: the next sentence switches to "tests them on work you've actually done" without linking the two, so the reader has to supply the missing connection.
reasons.GPT-5.6::D04. Analogy clicks without alg: It leads with the compressed line "a reference check for AI" and never says what corresponds to what, which is the failure pattern the rubric names.
reasons.GPT-5.6::D05. Make personal standards co: It mentions "your own judgment and corrections" and "what 'good' means to you" but gives no example of an actual standard, such as a headline being interesting or following AP style.
reasons.GPT-5.6::D07. Tests performance on your: It presents a personal benchmark as "a reference check for AI," which endorses the secondhand-report framing that Dan rejected in favor of a work trial, even though the paragraph also mentions testing on your work.
